name: 2 Thessalonians
author: The letter names Paul as its writer, together with his travelling companions Silas (also called Silvanus) and Timothy. Paul was a Jewish teacher from Tarsus, trained as a Pharisee (a strict keeper of Jewish law), who earned his living as a tentmaker and became a travelling missionary after coming to believe in Jesus. Traditionally the letter is accepted as Paul's own, written soon after 1 Thessalonians, though many scholars think a later follower wrote it in his name.
audience: It was written to a young church in Thessalonica, a busy port and the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia in northern Greece. Most members were non-Jews who had turned from local gods, and Paul had been forced to leave the city after only a short stay. The believers faced hostility from their neighbours and were unsettled by questions about the future.
era: If Paul wrote it, the date is around AD 50–51, probably from Corinth in southern Greece, during the reign of the emperor Claudius. Thessalonica sat on the Via Egnatia, a major Roman road linking east and west, and was a self-governing city loyal to Rome that honoured the emperor alongside its traditional gods. Small groups of Jesus-followers met in homes and often drew suspicion for abandoning the city's religious customs.

notes.1:3: This section speaks to believers who were still enduring persecution and hardship from people around them in Thessalonica.
notes.2:1: Some in the church had been alarmed by claims, possibly even a letter falsely said to be from Paul, that the 'day of the Lord' had already arrived.
notes.3:6: This addresses some church members who had stopped working and were living off the generosity of others.
notes.3:14: Letters were usually dictated to a scribe; here the writer adds a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark that the letter is genuine.

flags.problem: Wrong verse. The closing greeting in Paul's own hand is at 3:17. Verse 3:14 is about how to treat someone who ignores the letter's instructions, so a reader tapping this note at 3:14 would find it does not match the verse.
flags.suggestion: Move this note to 3:17. If a note is wanted at 3:14, write a separate setting note for that verse or drop it.

flags.problem: The term 'day of the Lord' is left unexplained. Many ordinary readers will not know what it refers to, so they may not see why the claim was alarming.
flags.suggestion: Add a short neutral gloss, e.g. 'the day of the Lord (the expected day when God would act decisively and Jesus would return)'.
